title: A Wife for Isaac: Rebekah at the Well
summary: Old Abraham makes his chief servant swear to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives in Mesopotamia, not among the Canaanites. At a well in Nahor's town the servant prays for a sign, and Rebekah, Abraham's great-niece, answers it by offering water to him and his camels. Her family agrees, Rebekah herself consents to go, and she travels to Canaan, where Isaac marries her and loves her.
story: Sarah has died (Genesis 23), Abraham is old, and Isaac is unmarried. The promise of descendants now depends on the next generation, and this chapter secures it. It is the longest chapter in Genesis, and it contains Abraham's last recorded words: his insistence that Isaac must not leave the land and his confidence that God's angel will go ahead of his servant (verses 6-8). The genealogy at the end of Genesis 22 already introduced Rebekah; now she steps into the story as a decisive, generous woman who will become the mother of Jacob and Esau. With Isaac comforted after his mother's death, the story is ready to move from Abraham to his son.
historical:
The servant travels to Aram-naharaim, meaning Aram of the two rivers, the region of upper Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and its tributaries, several hundred miles north and east of Canaan. His destination, Nahor's hometown, may mean the town where Nahor lived, which Genesis elsewhere links with Harran (Genesis 27:43; 29:4), or a town named Nahor; a place called Nahur appears in texts from Mari, the city on the middle Euphrates, from the early second millennium BC.

The ten camels raise a historical question. Archaeological work by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, widely reported in 2014, dated the earliest domesticated camel bones in the copper-mining region of the Arabah, south of the Dead Sea, to around the tenth century BC, and some scholars take this as a sign that the camel details reflect a later period. Others point to earlier evidence of camel domestication in Arabia and elsewhere and argue that a wealthy man could own a few camels long before they were common in Israel. The question is open, and it doesn't affect the story's point.
cultural:
The oath with the hand “under my thigh” (verse 2), repeated in Genesis 47:29, is usually understood as a gesture touching the organ of procreation, linking the oath to Abraham's descendants and perhaps to the covenant sign of circumcision. Marrying within the wider family was common and valued; Abraham's concern, though, is religious as much as tribal. His heir must not be absorbed into the Canaanites or leave the land God promised, and the later problems caused by Esau's Hittite wives (Genesis 26:34-35; 27:46) show why this mattered.

Wells were natural meeting places, and drawing water in the evening was women's work. Rebekah's offer to water ten camels after a long trek is extraordinary, since thirsty camels drink a great deal and every jar had to be hauled up by hand. The gold nose ring and bracelets, and the gifts to her brother and mother, belong to the exchange of gifts that accompanied betrothal. Her brother Laban plays a leading role in the negotiation, a sign of a brother's authority in his sister's marriage. The veil she puts on when she sees Isaac marks her as a bride coming to her husband.
literary: The chapter is a carefully paced story in five scenes, and it is full of repetition. The servant's prayer (verses 12-14) is fulfilled almost word for word (verses 17-20), and then he retells the whole story to Rebekah's family (verses 34-49). His retelling is not a copy. He leaves out Abraham's fear that Isaac might go back, stresses Abraham's wealth and God's blessing, and reverses the order of the gifts and the question about her family, presenting himself as having asked her lineage before giving her the ring. The storyteller trusts the reader to notice the diplomacy. Scholars such as Robert Alter have described the meeting of a future bride at a well as a recurring biblical type-scene: Jacob meets Rachel at a well (Genesis 29), and Moses meets Zipporah at one (Exodus 2). Here, unusually, the groom isn't present, and the servant, who is never named, acts for him. God never speaks in the chapter, yet everyone in it recognizes his hand.

outline.t: Abraham makes his servant swear an oath
Prayer at the well, and Rebekah's answer
Laban's welcome and the servant's account
The family agrees, and Rebekah chooses to go
Isaac and Rebekah meet and marry

doctrines.note: No miracle happens in this chapter, and God doesn't speak, yet the whole story is guided by him. The servant says “the LORD has led me” (verse 27), and Laban and Bethuel conclude, “This is from the LORD” (verse 50). God's providence often works through ordinary choices, timing, and character.
The servant prays specifically, before he has “finished praying” the answer arrives (verse 15), and he immediately bows and worships. Prayer and thanksgiving frame his whole errand.

Marriage here is part of God's larger purpose for a family and a people. The chapter also gives Rebekah a voice: asked whether she will go, she answers for herself, and the chapter ends with the plain statement that Isaac loved her.

words.note: Chesed, steadfast love, kindness, covenant loyalty: faithful love that goes beyond what is strictly owed. The servant asks God to show chesed to Abraham (verse 12) and praises him for not withholding it (verse 27). It becomes one of the Old Testament's great words for God's character.

Emet, faithfulness, truth, reliability. It is paired with chesed in verse 27, “His kindness and faithfulness,” a pair that recurs in Exodus 34:6 and throughout the Psalms to describe who God is. Chesed is love that commits; emet is the dependability that keeps the commitment.

Suach, the verb in verse 63 for what Isaac went out to the field to do. It occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. The BSB renders it meditate, following one ancient line of interpretation; others suggest walk, stroll, or even lament, which would suit his grief for his mother.

christ: This chapter secures the next link in the line of promise that leads through Isaac and Jacob to David and to Christ (Matthew 1:2). Rebekah's family blesses her with words that echo God's oath to Abraham in Genesis 22:17, that her offspring would “possess the gates of their enemies,” and Christians read that promise as fulfilled in the one offspring of Abraham who overcomes every enemy, including death. Many readers also notice that Jesus' conversation with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (John 4) draws on the well-meeting pattern that begins here, with Jesus in the place of the bridegroom offering living water. Some older Christian interpreters read the unnamed servant as a figure of the Holy Spirit bringing a bride to the Son; that is an allegorical reading, not something the text or the New Testament states. The broader picture of God seeking a bride for his Son does, however, belong to the New Testament's own imagery of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 19:7).

hard.q: Should Christians seek guidance by asking God for a sign, as the servant did?
hard.a:
The servant asked God to identify the right woman by a specific sign, and God answered at once. Some readers take this as a model for making decisions by asking for signs; others are wary, noting that Scripture also warns against putting God to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16) and that Gideon's repeated signs in Judges 6 come from weak faith.

The details of the chapter suggest a middle path. The sign the servant chose was not arbitrary, like a coin toss. It tested character: a woman who would offer a stranger water and then volunteer to water ten camels would be generous, hardworking, and hospitable, the kind of wife Isaac needed. The servant also acted with wisdom, going where Abraham told him, and he watched to see whether the answer was really from God before speaking (verse 21). Genesis describes what happened in this case rather than prescribing a method. Most Christian traditions teach that guidance ordinarily comes through Scripture, prayer, wisdom, and counsel, while acknowledging that God can and sometimes does answer specific requests, as he did here.

questions: God is never heard speaking in this chapter, yet everyone sees his hand. Where have you recognized God's guidance only by looking back?
Rebekah's generosity went far beyond what was asked. What does her example suggest about the kind of character that God's purposes often work through?
The servant worshiped the moment his prayer was answered. What would change if gratitude came as quickly as asking in your own life?
